claims.text: Adding approximately 3–5 at.% Hf to W-Ta-Cr-V will increase room-temperature strength.
Adding approximately 3–5 at.% Hf to W-Ta-Cr-V will improve room-temperature ductility.
The Hf-modified alloy will preserve the baseline alloy's high-temperature stability.
The Hf-modified alloy will preserve the baseline alloy's irradiation stability.
The baseline W-Ta-Cr-V alloy is nanocrystalline.
The baseline W-Ta-Cr-V alloy is a single-phase solid solution.
The baseline alloy has good thermal stability.
The baseline alloy has good irradiation stability.
The baseline alloy has limited room-temperature ductility.
The predicted performance improvement should manifest at temperatures of at least 900 K under ion or dual-beam irradiation.
Hf addition modifies lattice distortion in W-Ta-Cr-V.
Hf addition modifies short-range ordering in W-Ta-Cr-V.
Hf-induced lattice strain enhances solid-solution strengthening.
An Hf concentration of 3–5 at.% will not promote detrimental precipitate formation.
Hf addition modifies radiation-defect recombination kinetics.
Hf facilitates recombination of radiation-induced vacancies and interstitials.
Enhanced lattice distortion mitigates irradiation-induced defect accumulation.
The Hf-modified alloy will exhibit similar or less irradiation hardening than the baseline.
The Hf-modified alloy will maintain microstructural stability after long-term high-temperature irradiation.
Hf contents above the proposed range may cause segregation, brittle intermetallic formation, secondary-phase precipitation, or embrittlement.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis targets improved room-temperature mechanical performance, whereas the conditions say that improvement should manifest at temperatures of at least 900 K; the experiment does not specify whether mechanical testing occurs at room temperature or at the exposure temperature.
